title: What time do you get up?
goal: Tell the time, make appointments and describe your daily routine — and get the clock right from the start: *три и половина* is 3:30 ("three and a half"), never 2:30.
bekal: ask and tell the time with **и**, **без**, and **и половина**
name the days of the week

dialogs.title: Диалог — Making a date
dialogs.intro: Ivan wants to invite Ani to a show. Notice how times are expressed — and that *и половина* counts forward from the hour that's named.

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: What time do you get up in the morning?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: At seven. I have breakfast at seven-thirty.
lines.literal: at — seven. breakfast-I — at — seven — and — half.

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: And when do your classes start?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: At a quarter to nine. They finish at one.
lines.literal: at — nine — without — fifteen. finish-they — at — one.

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: So you're free in the afternoon.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Yes, but I usually study until five. After that I rest.
lines.literal: yes, but — usually — study-I — until — five. afterwards — rest-I.

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: Could we meet on Thursday evening?
lines.literal: may — (question) — that — each-other — see-we — on — Thursday — evening?

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: At seven-thirty, in front of the National Theater.
lines.literal: at — seven — and — half, in-front-of — National-the — theater.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: OK. But please, don't be late!
lines.literal: fine. but — beg-I — you, not — be-late-(command)!

notes: ⚠️ **Седем и половина means 7:30.** Literally "seven and a half", so it counts forward from the hour named — just like English "half past seven". If you've learned German or Dutch, beware: there *halb acht* means 7:30 too, but counts toward eight. **Safe rule: take the number you hear and add thirty minutes.** *Три и половина* = 3:30. *Дванайсет и половина* = 12:30.

**Без means "to" (literally "without"), and the hour comes FIRST.** *Девет без петнайсет* = "nine without fifteen" = 8:45. English says "a quarter to nine", with the hour last. ⚠️ Mishearing this means arriving an hour early or late, so practice reading a wall clock out loud.

**Часът means "the time" (o'clock); час means "an hour" as a length of time, and also "a class, a lesson".** *Колко е часът?* (What time is it?), *Уча два часа* (I study for two hours), *Часовете започват в девет* (Classes start at nine).

**В means "at" with times, and is pronounced f before a voiceless consonant.** *В седем* sounds like *f SEH-dem*, *в пет* like *f pet*. The spelling stays **в**. This applies to all one-letter prepositions.

**Да се видим literally means "that we see each other" and it means "to meet".** The word **се** means "oneself" or "each other", and it attaches to many Bulgarian verbs to change their meaning: *казвам* (say) → *казвам се* (be called), *връщам* (give back) → *връщам се* (come back), *виждам* (see) → *виждаме се* (meet).
**Моля те means "please" with a pleading tone, not just "here you are".** The formal form is *моля Ви*. Adding it instantly softens a request or a warning.

**Не закъснявай is a prohibition.** It's the command form for one person, made negative with *не*. For more than one person, or formally: *Не закъснявайте.* Commands are covered more fully in Unit 11.

**Никога не закъснявам uses two negatives at once**, and that's the correct form. *Никога* must be paired with *не*. Unit 13 covers it fully — for now, just accept that dropping either one makes the sentence wrong.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: In conversation Bulgarians use the 1–12 clock, adding *сутринта*, *следобед* or *вечерта* when needed. The 24-hour clock is used on train timetables and in official announcements.
after: There are two questions, and they mean different things: **Колко е часът?** asks what time it is now. **В колко часа?** asks what time something happens. Don't mix them up — the second always starts with *в*.

grammars.title: Verbs with се
body: Dozens of Bulgarian verbs carry **се** as a fixed part. It can't always be translated; sometimes it means "oneself", sometimes "each other", and sometimes it just changes the meaning of the verb.
after: **Се follows the same position rule as съм and ми**: it can't be the first word in a sentence, and it stays as close to its verb as possible. *Казвам се Ани*, not *Се казвам Ани*. In the *да* pattern it slips in between: *трябва да **се** върна*.

sections.title: A day from waking up to bedtime

blocks.text: Look at the three eating verbs: **закусвам, обядвам, вечерям** — one word each for having breakfast, lunch and dinner, with no need for the word "eat" at all. English mostly says "have breakfast"; Bulgarian packs it into a single verb.

Tonight, try describing your own day in six sentences, then read them out loud. A routine is the best practice material for the present tense, because you already know the content and only have to think about the forms.

The days are numbered, as in Portuguese or Hebrew: counting starts from the day after the rest day. *Неделя* — Sunday — literally means "no-work", from *не* + *дело* (work). And *понеделник* is "the day after no-work". Once you see the pattern, the seven names hardly need memorizing.

⚠️ **Days and months are never capitalized** in Bulgarian, except at the start of a sentence. The English habit of writing *Monday* and *March* with capitals doesn't apply here — and it's the most common spelling mistake learners make.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right verb form.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: пет часа — седем и половина — девет и петнайсет — дванайсет без петнайсет — дванайсет и половина — три без десет
В колко часа ставаш? — Закусвам в седем и половина. — В девет без петнайсет. — Може ли да се видим? — Никога не закъснявам.
Колко е часът? — Ставам в седем. — Часовете свършват в един. — Може ли да се видим в четвъртък? — Не закъснявай!
